DESIGN SPECIFICATION — Use case: illustration-story. Asset: finished Korean small museum exhibition poster. 요청한 화면 비율을 유지하면서 현재 도구와 모델이 지원하는 가능한 최대 해상도로 출력. Portrait width:height 2:3, opaque white canvas edge to edge.

Show the actual everyday relation of unlocking and opening ONE same door through TWO large calm human hand gestures. Pure black and white flat illustration, clear unbroken black contours around white hands, solid black metal hardware with localized broad smooth white wear patches. No photo, no 3D, no halftone, no paper grain, no sepia, no rust, no uniform distress, no horror mood. Everyday museum warmth comes from the familiar action and balanced shapes, not invented captions or decorative effects.

The door face and its narrow right vertical edge connect the upper lever pivot and lower circular lock cylinder at the same x position. A lever fixed to a visible round pivot at upper right extends left. A large forearm enters from the LEFT edge in the upper quarter and the hand naturally curls around the underside and rear of the lever, leaving part of its worn top contact surface visible. Keep recognizable fingers and thumb with plausible overlap, not a mitten or impossible extra fingers. The solid metal lever silhouette stays intact; its wear is a wide white polished patch following the upper curve, not a hole or broken edge.

Lower right, a second forearm enters from the RIGHT edge. Its thumb and index hold one side of a large ordinary key bow in a turning pinch. The intact opposite bow rim has a broad smooth white contact-wear strip. The key shaft visibly reaches and is inserted into the keyway in the lower cylinder, with a clear collar/contact boundary. Slight oblique hardware drawing makes shaft depth and insertion readable; no floating key or key laid flat on top of the cylinder. A portion of exposed shaft shows local polished wear. The lower cylinder has a visible outer rim fixed into the same door face. Do not add arrows, fingerprints, palm-print symbols, usage icons, invented collection IDs, dates, logos, sponsors, labels, ornaments or extra text.

COMPOSITION AND TYPE: The two large contact gestures create a central-left open reading area. The upper hand/lever scene fills about the upper third; the lower key/hand sits toward the right around the lower third. The door edge runs continuously at the right, keeping this ONE integrated door scene. The upper wrist crosses the left border; lower wrist crosses the right border. Adjust the lower wrist position to keep the entire supplied copy readable. Neither hand touches the letters.

Place the title centrally left between the arms, generous solid black Korean sans-serif with natural square Hangul proportions, crisp counters and ordinary word spacing. Use two horizontal lines at word boundaries: “손이 기억하는” then “물건”; no repeated title. The subtitle “열쇠와 손잡이의 생활사” immediately below in a smaller but substantial weight. Dates and place continue the same left alignment below. Hours, free admission and URL occupy a broad left reading area adjacent to the lower key, spanning a substantial vertical area rather than a tiny footer band. Reserve width for the longest hours and URL BEFORE sizing the drawing. Hours may wrap after the slash into two readable lines; do not break the actual example.org/hand-memory address. The URL entry may wrap between “전시 안내” and the intact URL only if needed. Keep body text proportionate, regular and confidently legible at 720px poster width. Do not horizontally squeeze letters or fill counters. About 8% horizontal text margins and stable line spacing, slightly stronger date/place than the practical hours. The central title, related action and practical info form one reading space bounded by the two gestures, not separate title/hero/footer stripes.

Print exactly all seven copy entries above once, no other copy. Every number, en dash, colon, slash and URL must be correct. The solid black/white illustration must be substantive and remain recognizable at thumbnail scale; the worn lever contact and worn key bow must remain visible beside the hands. No claims of any particular historical artifact, model, material or date.
